title.narrative: The NEST Project: Nonviolent Engagement for Safety and Security Transformation

description.narrative: Our efforts are organized around 3 themes that contribute to the overarching paradigm shift: Protection in transitional settings, localized protection responses, and gender in civilian protection.The protection gaps that emerge in transitional settings as conflicts change character and peacekeeping missions draw down present an urgent challenge and opportunity to guide key stakeholders. NP advocates for transitional strategies that are awake and responsive to protection gaps, resource violence prevention and protection through a UCP lens. Too often, protection responsibilities and civilian agency are abdicated in the wake of UN mission drawdowns.We draw on experience initiating protection efforts around the withdrawal of peacekeeping forces from Sudan and working alongside peacekeeping missions in South Sudan to highlight UCP approaches as one way of meeting civilian needs. DRC will also feature strongly amid the MONUSCO withdrawal.The role of local partnerships for protection is foundational to effective UCP. In crisis it is often civilians themselves who are first responders. Drawing on our experiences working alongside Women’s Protection Teams (WPTs) in South Sudan, and volunteer groups in Ukraine, this project enables us to further enhance locally led responses and deepen connections with mutual aid networks. We will use this direct experience to support international aid systems to integrate localization led by and for local people.There remains a critical need to explore the role of gender and other sources of marginalization in ongoing violence and protection responses – not just the impact of UCP interventions like WPTs, but also efforts to debunk the portrayal and treatment of men and boys as perpetrators alone. We take an intersectional approach, highlighting how interlocking forms of marginalization exacerbate risks for individuals facing violence. We will build on our extensive efforts in South Sudan with WPTs, gender champions, and SGBV programming, and combine our advocacy with enhancing leadership of women to drive policy change.

The three thematic priorities outlined above cut across target stakeholder groups. Though a range of stakeholders shape civilian protection policies and practice, institutionalization is subject to significant influence from three key spheres:a) The UN and member states shape civilian security through peacekeeping and conflict resolution. Their focus on the use of force as a tool has meant nonviolent approaches are under-researched and –resourced in protection toolkits. As pressure on conventional peacekeeping missions intensifies, with withdrawal of host state consent and mistrust from host populations toward missions, now is a critical time to advocate for approaches that center civilian agency.b) As the role of the UN shifts, regional blocs, including the EU, AU and MENA region are increasingly shaping civilian protection agendas. Whether through joint/complementary missions with the UN, security assistance (e.g. European Peace Facility), mediation, or less formal but nevertheless influential multilateral activity for conflict de-escalation in the MENA region, advocacy approaches for the advancement of civilian security must include these actors.c) Though often reluctant to grapple with their role in shaping security, INGOs are key players in shaping security for civilians in conflict-affected states. This category is intentionally broader than humanitarian organizations alone, as coordination across the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus is essential to address gaps in prevention and protection from violence. The solution is not sectoral, and civilian protection cannot be abandoned in ‘post-conflict’ environments.

The world is experiencing a surge of violent conflict and re-militarization. Authoritarian regimes have become more effective at co-opting and circumventing norms and institutions meant to protect basic liberties. Those in power tell us security can be maintained by isolating ourselves from others’ suffering, or by enclosing and eliminating the people who threaten our (way of) life.Ongoing cycles of violent conflict present a different picture, showing us that the idea of ‘security from the enemy other’ is not working. While armed approaches to security continue to play an important role, they are costly, externally imposed, ungrounded in local realities, and have heavy environmental and climate consequences. Moreover, their reliance on weapons and the use of force reinforces a culture of militarization. Armed peacekeepers are restricted by narrow mandates and struggle to address diverse civilian protection concerns. Protection provided by humanitarians is largely remedial, mitigating impact. Both the humanitarian protection and PoC agendas for change still inadequately appreciate the roles civilians can play in their own protection.NP has worked since its inception to facilitate alternative pathways to security through a practical, forward leaning and community-led approach to direct protection that is effective, affordable, and eco-friendly. While this approach – Unarmed Civilian Protection (UCP) - is increasingly recognized within peacekeeping and humanitarian communities, its lessons cannot be transferred easily, as systems change is necessary to reap its true benefits. The current system with its designated sectoral silos and linear logical frameworks is not set up for adaptive protection programming nor for conflict sensitivity to a be lived, enacted practice.A response aligned with the traditional mechanistic system would be to scale up NP’s own operations, but this would likely increase standardization and top-down implementation and is less sustainable in a rapidly changing world. Efforts to foster a global community around nonviolent approaches to security have gained traction, but it remains driven by Global North actors. Moreover, data is limited or not strategically aligned to remove specific policy barriers. All the while, more communities are requesting assistance in initiating their own protection efforts. The overarching goal that this project seeks to contribute to is a shift in focus among policy- and decision-makers in the security space away from force protection as a primary means of understanding and practicing security in violence-affected states, and toward an understanding of security that centers locally led, nonviolent, relational forms of security – including UCP – as an effective, strategic, and powerful practice for preventing and responding to conflict and security threats. Defenders of peace, human rights and nonviolent action need to work together in the sturdiest, widely possible coalitions to make this shift a reality.

We aim to advance the proposed shift through four mutually reinforcing objectives:1. Increase policy support, recognition, and funding for unarmed approaches for the security of people and communities.2. Enhance collective learning and critical evidence, and articulate exemplary, culturally appropriate models of unarmed approaches to security.3. Mobilize national and regional networks of practitioners, researchers, and supporters around unarmed approaches to security and nonviolence.4. Implement preventive and response actions that enhance the security of people and communities through nonviolent means.

recipient-country.narrative: In the past two years, those most affected have included those living in border areas with neighbouring countries due to attacks by armed groups, including M23, ADF, Red Tabara in South Kivu, Ituri and Tanganika. Despite ongoing insecurity, the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) is preparing a phased drawdown, beginning in South Kivu followed by North Kivu and Ituri. Amid a growing recognition of the utility of a UCP approach in the Congo, the policy influencing experience and partnerships that NP already has in hand provides a strong basis for NP’s planned efforts to strengthen and mobilize local protection teams in areas where protection gaps are felt most acutely. This implementation, in turn, greatly enhances our efforts to influence peacekeeping policy and understandings of civilian needs and responses to protection risks in transitional conflict settings.

Iraq has a long history of sectarian disputes, exclusion of ethnic-religious groups from decision-making, and power asymmetries leading to violent conflict. It has been further destabilized by atrocities committed under Daesh's rule. The past two decades have witnessed widespread violence, displacement, and profound societal rifts, deeply impacting the psychosocial wellbeing of citizens. Efforts to recover from these events and repair social fabric are hindered by the ongoing exclusion of entire communities from participation in peace and security processes. Very few civilians (save predominantly influential, older males from nonminority groups and dominant tribes) play an active role in peace and security processes. This exclusion perpetuates a cycle of trauma and marginalization, exacerbating psychological and social strains on the Iraqi population, and further fueling insecurity, actual and perceived.As conflicts progress from crisis and peace processes to post-conflict development, security threats often focus more on specific individuals within civil society. In Iraq, civil society groups face significant challenges such as intimidation, harassment, and marginalization in ahostile environment. NP is well placed to support communities to establish and implement unarmed, locally led security processes and frameworks that better represent all community segments and better address their unique safety and protection concerns. This effort is supported by strengthening the capacities and networks of civil society, coupled with the establishment of advocacy channels that urge policy makers to be more responsive to the security competencies of communities.

Since escalation in April 2023, Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its allied militias have swiftly taken control across West, Central, South and parts of North Darfur, with widespread human rights abuses and atrocities reported in the process, frequently along ethnic lines. While about 1.2 million people have fled to neighboring countries such as Chad and South Sudan, the vast majority, 5 million people, are displaced within Sudan, putting enormous pressure on already impoverished host communities. With an ailing UN-led response plan (fulfilled to only 33% of funding needs) and access restrictions for many international NGOs and the UN, the response in Sudan is often being led by and for civilians themselves. Decentralized mutual aid networks – known as emergency response rooms (ERRs) – have stepped in to fill the vacuum. Local capacities have far outweighed abilities of national and international structures – be this for solutions for security or humanitarian response. Despite this, documentation of local efforts, programming modalities to support them,and opportunities for local structures to engage with policy frameworks has been extremely limited. This has led to calls from the humanitarian community to shift operations toward centering local volunteer-led networks.

South Sudan continues to be plagued by systemic violence and insecurity. Despite the Revitalized Peace Agreement signed in September 2018, South Sudan faces sustained sub-national and intercommunal violence, human rights violations including sexual and gender-based violence, a weak judicial system, and exacerbated socio-economic hardships. The trauma of decades-longviolence and displacement, coupled with the loss of homes, livelihoods, and loved ones, significantly impacts the mental health of individuals and communities. Pressures on communities have recently been exacerbated by mass returns from Sudan, with an estimated 520,000 returnees expected to have arrived in South Sudan by early 2024 (per UNHCR). The presence of returnees has and will continue to sharpen existing resource and social challenges in South Sudan. Considering the deeply rooted cycles of violence, South Sudan’s aid dependency, decreasing level of global aid and development funds, and increasing crises elsewhere, it is easy to give up on South Sudan. The solution will not be found through investing in the status quo of aid and hard security. While cycles of violence have deep roots, there is also a growing momentum among individuals and groups standing up against impunity and modelling a culture of nonviolence by protecting civilians without the use of weapons or reliance on the threat of force that if fully invested in will contribute to shifting the paradigm.
